title: Big Tech, Embedded Finance and Open Finance
summary: An eight-module programme equipping supervisors to assess big tech, embedded finance and open finance models, and their concentration, conduct and operational risks.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to oversee the platform-driven reshaping of financial services: assessing big tech and embedded finance business models, banking-as-a-service partnerships, open finance data sharing and the concentration, conduct and operational risks they create.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a clear understanding of how large technology platforms, embedded finance providers and open finance ecosystems deliver financial services, and where accountability and risk sit along the value chain. Participants leave able to map platform and partnership models, challenge regulated firms and their partners, and contribute to the authority's approach to the perimeter, data access and cross-authority cooperation.
sections.What It Covers: Platform business models in finance, embedded finance and banking-as-a-service, data access and open finance, activity-based and entity-based regulation, concentration, competition and financial stability, operational dependency on platforms, consumer outcomes in digital journeys, and supervising platforms and partnerships in practice.
Intended Audience: Supervisors of banks, payment and e-money institutions, lenders and insurers that partner with platforms or distribute through them
Policy, innovation and authorisation staff dealing with new entrants, perimeter questions and open finance
Senior managers coordinating with competition, data protection and consumer authorities
Learning Objectives: Explain how big tech platforms and embedded finance providers enter and operate in financial services
Assess banking-as-a-service and distribution partnerships, including accountability for outsourced customer relationships
Evaluate open finance data-sharing frameworks and the risks of data concentration
Analyse the case for activity-based and entity-based approaches to regulating platforms
Identify concentration, operational dependency and consumer harm risks arising from platform finance
Design a supervisory approach to platforms and partnerships, including cooperation with other authorities
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with case studies and supervisory question exercises, closing with a partnership review workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of banking, payments or conduct supervision is helpful. No technical background is required.
Core Reading: FSB, Enhancing Third-Party Risk Management and Oversight: A Toolkit for Financial Institutions and Financial Authorities (2023)
G20/OECD High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection (2022)
FSB, Enhancing Cross-border Payments: Stage 3 Roadmap (2020)

modules.title: Platform Business Models in Finance
modules.summary: How large technology platforms enter financial services, the data, network and activity loop that drives their advantage, and how their models differ from traditional financial firms.
objectives: Explain the economics of platforms and the data-network-activities loop
Distinguish the routes by which big tech enters payments, credit, insurance and wealth
Identify where platform models create new supervisory challenges
syllabus: Network effects, ecosystems and cross-subsidisation
Entry routes: own licence, partnership or acquisition
Platform finance in advanced and emerging economies
BIS and FSB analysis of big tech in finance

modules.title: Embedded Finance and Banking-as-a-Service
modules.summary: How financial products are embedded into non-financial journeys and delivered through banking-as-a-service partnerships, and where regulatory responsibility sits when the customer relationship is outsourced.
objectives: Map the roles of licensed providers, platforms and intermediaries in embedded finance
Assess the sponsor firm's oversight of partners and programme managers
Evaluate red flags in fast-growing banking-as-a-service arrangements
syllabus: Embedded payments, lending, insurance and investment
Banking-as-a-service: sponsor banks, programme managers and middleware
Partner onboarding, AML/CFT controls and reconciliation of client funds
Case studies: partnership failures and supervisory findings

modules.title: Data Access and Open Finance
modules.summary: How open banking and open finance frameworks enable customer-permissioned data sharing, the design choices behind them, and the competition, privacy and security trade-offs supervisors need to understand.
objectives: Explain the design of open banking and open finance frameworks
Assess consent, liability and security arrangements for data sharing
Evaluate the risk that data access entrenches rather than reduces platform power
syllabus: Open banking to open finance: scope and data categories
APIs, standards, consent dashboards and liability models
Data protection, fraud and cybersecurity risks in data sharing
Reciprocity and data flows between big tech and incumbents

modules.title: Activity-Based and Entity-Based Regulation
modules.summary: Why the perimeter struggles with platforms that combine regulated and unregulated activities, and the arguments for activity-based rules, entity-based requirements or a combination of the two.
objectives: Compare activity-based and entity-based approaches to regulating platforms
Analyse perimeter gaps created by unregulated activities within platform groups
Evaluate group-level and holding company options for large platforms
syllabus: Same activity, same risk, same regulation: strengths and limits
Entity-based requirements for systemically relevant platforms
Mixed-activity groups and intragroup dependencies
FSB and BIS work on regulatory approaches to big tech

modules.title: Concentration, Competition and Financial Stability
modules.summary: How platform scale, data advantages and partnership networks can concentrate risk and market power, and when platform finance becomes a financial stability concern.
objectives: Analyse concentration risks in distribution, data and infrastructure
Assess the interaction between competition and financial stability objectives
Identify indicators that a platform has become systemically relevant
syllabus: Market power, lock-in, self-preferencing and data advantages
Rapid deposit and credit flows through platform channels
Interconnections with banks, funds and payment systems
Coordination with competition authorities

modules.title: Operational Dependency and Third-Party Risk
modules.summary: How financial firms' reliance on platforms for distribution, cloud, data and customer interfaces creates operational dependency, and how supervisors assess resilience and exit options.
objectives: Assess firms' operational dependency on platform partners and providers
Evaluate contractual rights, oversight and exit planning for critical platform relationships
Apply operational resilience principles to embedded and platform-based services
syllabus: Distribution dependency and loss of the customer interface
Cloud, data and technology dependencies on platform groups
Contractual rights, audit access and substitutability
Links to critical third-party oversight regimes

modules.title: Consumer Outcomes on Digital Platforms
modules.summary: How platform design, personalisation and data use shape consumer decisions, the risks of harm and exclusion, and the evidence supervisors should seek on outcomes in embedded journeys.
objectives: Identify consumer harms from choice architecture, dark patterns and frictionless credit
Assess disclosure, suitability and complaints handling in embedded journeys
Evaluate the financial inclusion benefits and risks of platform finance
syllabus: Choice architecture, defaults and dark patterns
Embedded credit and buy now, pay later products
Personalised pricing, profiling and fair treatment
Who owns the complaint: redress across the partnership chain

modules.title: Supervising Platforms and Partnerships in Practice
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a practical supervisory approach to platforms and partnerships, from data and early warning indicators to cooperation with other authorities and the authority's policy stance.
objectives: Apply a supervisory assessment framework to a platform partnership
Evaluate cooperation arrangements with competition, data protection and consumer authorities
Design priorities for the authority's approach to platform finance
syllabus: Mapping partnership chains and accountability
Early warning indicators and thematic reviews of partnerships
Cross-authority and cross-border cooperation
Workshop: supervisory review of an embedded finance partnership

related.title: Digital Operational Resilience under DORA (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on DORA for supervisors and financial entities: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and TLPT, ICT third-party risk and critical provider oversight.

related.title: Operational Resilience, Cyber and Critical Third Parties
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' operational resilience, cyber risk, incident response and third-party dependencies, and to shape the authority's resilience strategy.

related.title: Quantum and Cryptographic Resilience
related.summary: A six-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' exposure to quantum threats, cryptographic inventories and post-quantum migration plans, and to set proportionate expectations.

related.title: Digital Money: Stablecoins, Tokenised Deposits and CBDCs
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and central bankers to assess stablecoins, tokenised deposits and CBDCs, and their risks to payments and financial stability.

related.title: EU Payments Regulation: PSD2, PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on EU payments regulation for supervisors and firms, covering PSD2 and EMD2 today and the PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation reform package.

related.title: Payment Services Supervision
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to authorise and supervise payment and e-money institutions, from safeguarding and fraud to open banking, instant payments and wind-down.
